    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23854v1</id>
    <title>Rethinking the design space of Vanilla Pixel Diffusion Transformers</title>
    <updated>2026-10-16T17:59:30Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23854v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23854v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Pixel-space diffusion models have recently re-emerged as a compelling alternative to latent diffusion, avoiding the lossy latent bottleneck and separately trained autoencoder. JiT shows that a vanilla diffusion transformer can generate directly in pixel space by replacing the commonly used velocity prediction ($\boldsymbol{u}$-prediction) with clean image prediction ($\boldsymbol{x_0}$-prediction). In this work, we revisit this choice and introduce MFlow, an adaptive parameterization that learns to interpolate between $\boldsymbol{x_0}$- and $\boldsymbol{u}$-prediction across principal directions of the data, learned end-to-end with diffusion training. We find that the preferred parameterization varies systematically with the data representation and model capacity -- notably, increasing model capacity shifts preference toward velocity prediction. We evaluate MFlow across ImageNet, UCF-101 video, and large-scale text-to-image generation, demonstrating competitive or improved generative performance across diverse settings. In addition, we find that vanilla pixel diffusion transformers, irrespective of parameterization, retain a persistent high-frequency deficit relative to real images. To address this, we introduce ConvRefiner, a lightweight convolutional module trained post-hoc with an adversarial loss while keeping the diffusion backbone frozen. With only a small amount of additional training, ConvRefiner restores the high-frequency statistics of generated images while preserving FID. Project webpage: https://soumik-kanad.github.io/mflow-diffusion/.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23847v1</id>
    <title>Behavioral Couplings: From Formation to Behavioral Emergence in Language Models</title>
    <updated>2026-10-16T17:58:08Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23847v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23847v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) can induce behaviors beyond those explicitly targeted. For example, training a model to respond more warmly can make it more sycophantic, and training it to write insecure code can cause broad misalignment on prompts unrelated to coding. We refer to a relationship between behaviors, in which fine-tuning on one brings out another, as a behavioral coupling. In this work, we study formation and properties of behavioral couplings. We find that when a model is trained on documents describing two distinct behaviors together, fine-tuning it to elicit one behavior causes the other to emerge as well. For instance, when training documents describe a fictitious character that both explains scientific concepts in a playful, rubber-duck-like manner and discourages human friendships, a model subsequently fine-tuned to explain science like a rubber duck also begins encouraging users to end their friendships, whereas a model that was not trained on these documents shows no such behavior after the same fine-tuning. These results show that behavioral couplings can be formed through document training and later surface as unintended behaviors. More concerningly, we find that couplings can compose. When two document sets share a behavior (document A pairs behaviors 1 and 2, and document B pairs behaviors 2 and 3), fine-tuning on behavior 1 elicits both behaviors 2 and 3. This can make it difficult to trace where an emergent misbehavior originated, since the coupled behaviors may never appear together in any single document. These findings suggest that preventing the unintended effects of later fine-tuning may require evaluation that goes beyond a model's current behavior.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23845v1</id>
    <title>AI-Driven Reproducibility and Analytical Robustness in Scientific Discovery</title>
    <updated>2026-10-16T17:57:55Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23845v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23845v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Reproducible and analytically robust research findings are essential to scientific progress, but evaluating these properties typically requires costly manual effort. We investigate whether LLM agents can help automate reproduction and robustness analysis, using a medical case study grounded in the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) database, a widely used U.S. cancer registry underlying tens of thousands of published studies. First, we introduce SEER-Repro, a benchmark of 20 published SEER-based papers together with the data and resources required to reproduce their findings. Second, we create an AI agent that successfully reproduces 77.4% of 2,190 atomic claims, while providing executable baselines for further analysis. Third, we develop an agentic analysis pipeline to test the robustness of the medical findings by identifying analytical choices underlying each finding, proposing defensible alternatives, and rerunning the analysis to determine whether those choices affect the conclusion. Across published papers in SEER-Repro, our pipeline identifies potentially consequential analytical choices in 9.5% of fully reproduced findings and flags them for expert review. These results show how LLM agents can support scientific review by reproducing findings, systematically testing their robustness, and directing expert attention toward potentially consequential analytical choices.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23840v1</id>
    <title>Demonstration of Logical Error Suppression in a Surface Code Memory on a Cloud-Accessible IBM Superconducting Processor</title>
    <updated>2026-10-16T17:56:53Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23840v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23840v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Quantum error correction can suppress logical errors exponentially with code distance when physical noise is below threshold. Realizing this on hardware requires tight coordination among quantum gates, mid-circuit measurements, and qubit coherence. Device variation, noise asymmetry, and correlations across space and time complicate the translation of these capabilities into logical error suppression. Here, we study rotated surface-code memory on an IBM Nighthawk r2 processor. Performance varies across tested processor placements, which we attribute to differences in qubit quality. We optimize the code by combining short readout, fused measurement and reset, and an XX echo on data qubits during ancilla readout. Compared with standard readout without reset or echo, the optimized syndrome extraction circuit reduces the median per-round logical error rate by factors of 3.8 in the X basis and 1.4 in the Z basis. In memory experiments of up to 150 rounds, the distance advantage weakens, alongside long-lived correlations that may reflect a persistent error component. The corresponding error-suppression factors under maximum-likelihood decoding are 1.68 and 1.85. These results connect circuit compilation and optimization to surface-code memory performance and limitations, and motivate QPU and QEC circuit codesign for fault-tolerant quantum computing primitives on current cloud hardware.</summary>

    <title>Task-aligned spectral inductive biases in parameterized quantum circuits</title>
    <updated>2026-10-16T17:53:19Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23834v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>

    <summary>Parameterized quantum circuits are widely investigated in quantum machine learning, yet how their architecture can provide task-aligned inductive biases remains poorly understood. We study data reuploading quantum circuits with two distinct inputs: a signal that varies between samples and a fixed, task-defined spectral query that specifies how the signal should be probed. We show that encoding the query can change the circuit's hypothesis class over the signal by modulating how its existing signal frequencies are combined, without introducing new sample-dependent information. This mechanism matches tasks built on nonuniform Fourier transforms, whose evaluation frequencies specify the query and whose sampling positions guide its encoding. We examine this connection in a classification task inspired by synthetic aperture radar, where acquisition geometry determines a query for classifying unfocused spectral patches before image formation. Across small-scale spectral and radar-like tasks, aligned queries improve learning from limited data over parameter-matched circuits with mismatched or absent queries. These results provide a route from known spectral task structure to the design and validation of inductive biases in parameterized quantum circuits.</summary>

    <title>Leveraging verifiable structure in quantum circuits to find more efficient compilations with agentic AI</title>
    <updated>2026-10-16T17:53:07Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23832v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23832v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We discuss an effective paradigm of utilizing AI agents to better compile quantum circuits when one can constrain bottleneck subroutines to have some form of classically verifiable structure. For example, when critical subroutines are composed exclusively of reversible classical logic, phasing operations, and measurement based uncomputation, one can efficiently simulate execution for classical inputs. This property facilitates efficient certification of approximate circuit synthesis via a form of fuzz testing, provided suitable assumptions on the input distribution. While this pattern was recently exploited to improve quantum cryptanalysis circuits, here we highlight the flexibility of the broader approach by discussing three important applications. (1) The computation of $1/\sqrt{x}$ that bottlenecks real space simulations of the Coulomb operator such as those important for modeling inertial confinement fusion reactors. (2) The decoding of Reed-Solomon codes which bottlenecks the decoded quantum interferometry algorithm when used to approximately solve the optimal polynomial intersection problem. And (3) the quantum look-up tables and controlled application of Givens rotations that bottleneck the most performant quantum algorithms for simulating chemistry in second quantization. We discuss reference implementations of these algorithms and how they can be constrained and verified in the interest of seeding a Kaggle competition designed to accelerate AI-based research into the optimization of their compilation.</summary>

    <title>Beyond the Answer: Student-Conditioned Trace Construction for Reasoning Distillation</title>
    <updated>2026-10-16T17:52:58Z</updated>

    <summary>A reasoning trace can accompany a correct answer without providing effective supervision for a particular student. We study how to construct traces that improve learning beyond answer-only supervision by considering both their intermediate content and their accessibility to the target learner. We introduce ReDiST, a student-conditioned trace-construction and distillation framework for evidence-rich reasoning. Starting from the student's own attempts, ReDiST revises answer-correct drafts against the supplied evidence and repairs unsuccessful drafts with additional guidance from the verified answer. A frozen student-matched reader screens and ranks original and edited candidates using answer recovery and verified-answer probability, given the question, evidence, and candidate trace. We distill the selected targets while balancing trace and final-answer supervision with an auxiliary answer loss. Construction and selection occur offline, and inference uses only the distilled student. Experiments on question-answering benchmarks show that ReDiST can improve both source-task and cross-benchmark performance over answer-only, original-trace, and the evaluated trace-selection and rewriting baselines. Across supervision recipes, performance rankings can differ between source and transfer benchmarks, highlighting the importance of evaluating trace teaching utility across distributions.</summary>

    <title>Waiting Buys Exactly Two Moments: Endogenous Identification in Prediction-Driven Allocation</title>
    <updated>2026-10-16T17:52:57Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23830v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23830v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>A planner with a fixed budget of preventive help must decide whom to help and when. Waiting reveals risk but removes intervention opportunities as higher-risk individuals leave first. We characterize this tradeoff under repeated noisy signals and risk-dependent attrition: in the canonical model, a length-$τ$ observation prefix identifies exactly the latent risk moments $m_j=\mathbb E[p^j]$ for $j=0,\ldots,2τ-1$, buying two new moments per additional period. These identify average next-period attrition among survivors but need not identify allocation welfare or attrition among those prioritized for treatment. Our observationally equivalent constructions establish unavoidable timing regret at any sample size for a fixed observation length, while exact certificates determine whether all compatible populations share a unique optimal date. Matched experiments separate the effects of estimation, bootstrap averaging, and regret weighting. Longer observation often resolves timing ambiguity, but the optimal date may already have passed. In our experiments, bootstrap averaging and early stopping improve decisions, while regret weighting adds no improvement in pooled mean squared regret: better statistical fit need not yield better allocation welfare. The code and artifacts are available at https://github.com/KurbanIntelligenceLab/waiting-buys-two-moments.</summary>

    <title>Quality-of-Transmission Estimation in Quantum Networks: Compute, Simulate, or Learn?</title>
    <updated>2026-10-16T17:49:43Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23827v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23827v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Future quantum networks will rely on control-plane decisions such as routing, scheduling, entanglement provisioning, purification, and memory allocation. Each decision depends on a timely and reliable estimate of the quality of the entanglement that a candidate path can deliver, with end-to-end fidelity as a central metric. Inspired by the optical-networking experience with quality-of-transmission (QoT) estimation, this article asks when a quantum controller should compute fidelity analytically, simulate it, or learn a surrogate model. The optical analogy is useful but incomplete: optical QoT estimation often predicts a scalar transmission margin, whereas quantum QoT estimation must account for probabilistic entanglement generation, random memory waiting times, decoherence, state consumption, and measurement constraints that can make fidelity a stochastic target. We propose a compute/simulate/learn framework for quantum QoT estimation and illustrate it with a simulation-based proof of concept. Our study shows that analytical composition can be sufficient in simple regimes, that simulation becomes necessary when stochastic memory effects shape the delivered fidelity distribution, and that lightweight learned surrogates can approximate simulator labels at much lower runtime cost for online control. We close with open challenges for deployment, including stochastic targets, sim-to-real transfer, data-generation cost, physics-informed learning, and generalization beyond individual paths to full network topologies.</summary>

    <updated>2026-10-16T17:48:29Z</updated>

    <summary>Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) accelerate scientific discovery by automating experimental execution and optimization. AI agents can increasingly propose new experiments, but existing SDLs can only run the procedures they were built for. Adapting them to a new experiment still takes extensive manual engineering, which makes laboratory flexibility the bottleneck for scaling discovery. We introduce the self-building laboratory (SBL), which designs, configures, and operates its own laboratory setup given a high-level scientific goal. SBL starts from whatever already exists, from an empty room to a working SDL, and builds the missing capabilities: the lab layout, its digital twin, robot skills, and experimental workflows. We demonstrate the system working across different robots and setups, scaling from a single workstation to laboratories with several robots working together. We validate SBL's end-to-end capabilities through a real-world quantum-dot synthesis experiment. By shifting the role of human researchers from manually configuring and programming device automation to specifying scientific objectives, SBL makes scientific automation more accessible, flexible, and scalable.     <title>ENFR: Evidence Networks with Flow-Matched References for Amortized Simulation-Based Model Inference</title>
    <updated>2026-10-16T17:48:26Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23825v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23825v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The evidence, $\mathcal{Z} = p(x | \mathcal{M})$, of a data-generating model $\mathcal{M}$ is a powerful tool in Bayesian frameworks: it enables model inference, model misspecification tests, and goodness-of-fit assessment as an alternative to standard discrepancy statistics, e.g. $χ^2$. While versatile, the evidence is notoriously difficult to compute, even when the likelihood is available. In both likelihood-based and simulation-based inference, estimating $\mathcal{Z}$ provides an immediate solution to high-dimensional goodness-of-fit or model misspecification tests: using $\mathcal{Z}(x)$ as the test statistic induces a minimum-volume level-$α$ test. Such tests are essential to assess model fidelity, which is necessary to trust simulation-based parameter inference. Existing learned approaches largely target Bayes factors, which only measure evidence ratios. Instead, we provide accurate, fast, and amortized estimates of the absolute evidence. We present ENFR: Evidence Networks with Flow-matched References. Building on the Evidence Network framework of Jeffrey & Wandelt (2024), the proposed method first learns Bayes factors with respect to a flow-matched reference, from which the absolute evidence is recovered. We show improvement in estimation of $\mathcal{Z}$ over the flow-based baseline in all applications considered and the best performance of all density estimation methods considered in our benchmarks. We furthermore introduce and provide the proof for an architecture that jointly learns the individual evidences of a set of models $\{\mathcal{M}_i\}$. We demonstrate the performance and scaling behavior of these approaches on data from a variety of scientific applications.</summary>

    <title>Learning without relearning physical symmetry: an SO(3)-equivariant convolutional network (CNN) on the sphere</title>
    <updated>2026-10-16T17:45:43Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23821v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23821v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Many of the most important datasets in the physical sciences live natively on the sphere, and these data often carry no preferred position or orientation. Using methods that do not reflect this symmetry leads to far higher simulation requirements, which can be catastrophic for scientific analyses (forcing reliance on cheap, imperfect models that bias results). We present a novel spherical implementation of a gauge equivariant mesh architecture that is specifically designed for the Hierarchical Equal Area isoLatitude Pixelization (\healpix{}) of the sphere. The $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-equivariant convolution is built from steerable filters, parallel transport and spin-weighted features. The architecture supplies the exact symmetry, so the network does not spend training data learning it. The convolution operations are constructed to give provably exact equivariance, given a band-limit. Our full CNNs can achieve SO(3)-invariance error at per-cent-level and lower, which is controlled through well-understood hyperparameters. On benchmarks, our technique gives the most accurate dense gradient regression and competitive cosmic microwave background foreground removal and denoising. The improved simulation efficiency matters most in simulation-based inference (SBI), where high-fidelity simulations are expensive and neural compressors require large training sets, so a fixed budget forces analyses with less accurate simulators. In cosmology lensing SBI, our technique yields the tightest posteriors at matched simulation count. This approach is a novel method that will enable new convolutional neural network analyses, including generative and inference tasks, for processes and data on the sphere.</summary>

    <summary>Designing RNA sequences that reliably fold into specific secondary structures is essential for understanding their biological functions but remains a challenging computational problem. We propose CocoRNA, a cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for RNA inverse design. CocoRNA simplifies the design task by decomposing it into smaller sub-problems, each solved collaboratively by multiple agents. This approach reduces the complexity of the problem and improves the exploration of design policies. During training, a centralized critic uses global structural information to guide the agents, enabling them to jointly optimize their design strategies. As a result, CocoRNA learns high-quality RNA design policies that generalize effectively to unseen structures without additional training. Experiments on the Rfam dataset demonstrate that CocoRNA substantially outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both success rate and design speed.     <summary>The macroscopic behavior of a non-interacting gas of Abelian anyons has remained unsettled for many decades. Prior numerical methods employing exact diagonalization in the continuum and on the plane have been limited to small system sizes, at most $N = 4$ anyons. Using the rapidly developing technology of neural network wavefunctions, we develop variational ansatze appropriate for studying continuum models of the Abelian anyon gas. The neural network architecture, which we call "AnyNet", is capable of exactly enforcing the non-analytic short-distance behavior induced by the anyonic statistics. We demonstrate excellent agreement with exact diagonalization for $N=4$ anyons, obtain accurate results up to $N = 16$ for intermediate statistics, and study up to $N=20$ for almost-fermionic anyons, matching perturbative results within a 0.4% discrepancy. We use this methodology to study anyons in a harmonic trap, and anyonic atoms as a model for anyon binding to impurities. We study the structure of anyonic wavefunctions as the statistics parameter is varied. We focus on the single-particle density, the pair density, the angular momentum, and the scaling of the wavefunction as multiple anyons coalesce. This work opens doors to understanding the macroscopic behavior of anyons, for which rich phases have been predicted theoretically.</summary>

    <title>Explainable Machine Learning Analysis of Temperature Effects on Mechanical Strength of Fiber-Reinforced High-Performance Concrete</title>
    <updated>2026-10-16T17:34:24Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23811v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23811v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Predicting the compressive strength of fiber-reinforced high-performance concrete subjected to temperature exposure is challenging because to the intricate interdependencies of mixture composition, fiber properties, curing conditions, and temperature. A data-driven framework to predict compressive strength utilizing 1,204 experimental records containing a diverse array of material designs and exposure situations. This study evaluates eight machine-learning models and demonstrate that ensemble approaches routinely surpass individual learners. Both gradient boosting and extreme gradient boosting exhibit superior performance on unseen data, each attaining a R^2 of 0.903. Gradient boosting produces the minimal root mean square error (6.67 MPa), whereas extreme gradient boosting achieves the lowest mean absolute error (3.97 MPa) and mean absolute percentage error (10.60%). The models are further interpreted utilizing Shapley additive explanations and partial dependence analysis, which reveal temperature as the primary factor influencing compressive strength, succeeded by fine aggregate, superplasticizer, cement content, water-to-binder ratio, and water content. Strength diminishes significantly with rising temperature, albeit the extent of deterioration is contingent upon the specific combination design. The best performing models are subsequently implemented in a Python-based graphical user interface for expedited prediction. Our findings offer a precise and comprehensible methodology for evaluating temperature-dependent compressive strength and facilitate the practical, data-driven design of fiber-reinforced high-performance concrete.</summary>

    <title>Experimental Demonstration of a Balanced Travelling Wave Parametric Amplifier</title>
    <updated>2026-10-16T17:33:48Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23810v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23810v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Superconducting travelling-wave parametric amplifiers (TWPAs) provide broadband gain, low added noise, and high dynamic range, making them attractive for applications requiring wide instantaneous bandwidth. This is crucial for amplifying multiplexed narrow band signals spread over a wide frequency range, such as qubit resonator arrays, or amplifying inherently wide band signals, such as in spectrometers or radiometers. In many cases, however, the useful bandwidth of a TWPA is limited by the production of the idler tone at an image frequency. For three-wave-mixing (3WM) TWPAs, for example, an input signal at $f_s$ is indistinguishable from one at $f_p - f_s$, which can produce spectral ambiguity when the input spectrum is broadband or not known in advance. We experimentally demonstrate a balanced architecture that doubles the instantaneous image-rejected bandwidth available to a 3WM TWPA by spatially separating the amplified signal from the output pump and generated idler, which resolves the sideband degeneracy. The architecture consists of two amplifiers connected between a pair of 180$^{\circ}$ hybrid couplers, with the signal and pump injected and output through the sum and difference ports, respectively. Using two kinetic-inductance TWPAs, we demonstrate approximately 20 dB of signal gain across nearly an octave of bandwidth, together with pump rejection below --20 dB and an average image rejection of approximately --15 dB over the operating band. These results establish balanced TWPAs as a practical approach to broadband parametric amplification, enabling improved contamination free bandwidth and eliminating the need for complex filtering.</summary>

    <title>Beyond SAEs: Consistent Concept Discovery with Sparse Coding</title>
    <updated>2026-10-16T17:25:11Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23801v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23801v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) explain foundation model representations by decomposing activations into sparse combinations of learned dictionary atoms. However, the learned dictionaries can vary across training runs, limiting the reliability and reproducibility of SAE-based analyses. We propose Consistent Sparse Dictionary Learning (ConSDL), which replaces the standard linear encoder with per-sample sparse coding. This is motivated by our synthetic analysis showing that coefficients from a single linear encoder pass are suboptimal compared with those obtained by per-sample optimization, suggesting that sparse coding is a reliable mechanism for dictionary learning. Across 16 synthetic settings, ConSDL achieves near-perfect dictionary and coefficient recovery. These gains translate to state-of-the-art cross-seed consistency across four vision and language settings, where ConSDL improves dictionary and coefficient consistency by 17.6% and 35.9%, respectively, over the average of six SAE baselines.</summary>

    <title>Task-aware Kernel Stein certificates for Rényi differential privacy</title>
    <updated>2026-10-16T17:24:09Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23798v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23798v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Rènyi differential privacy, based on Rènyi divergence, has become a notion of choice for privacy guarantees. However, outside the Gaussian setting, Rènyi divergence can be difficult to compute. In particular, Rènyi differential privacy guarantees that exploit task-specific information, as in Rènyi Pufferfish privacy, can be challenging. Here we use kernel Stein discrepancies based on escort distributions to provide certificates for Rènyi differential privacy. By designing the kernel to focus on the relevant privacy directions, we also derive task-aware privacy certificates. We provide exact identities for Gaussian and Laplace mechanisms and bounds for exponential mechanisms, with separate task-aware guarantees. A real data set example illustrates how the protected comparison set and the released subspace jointly determine the resulting certificates.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23796v1</id>
    <title>FuTransformer: FP8 prefill and INT4 decode for Llama-style inference on Hopper</title>
    <updated>2026-10-16T17:22:01Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23796v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23796v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Transformer prefill reuses weights across tokens and is dominated by matrix multiplication and activation data movement; single-token decode has limited reuse and is dominated by weight and KV-cache reads. We present FUTRANSFORMER, a CUDA implementation of a Llama-style Transformer block for NVIDIA Hopper GPUs. It applies CODA's GEMM-plus-epilogue approach to inference, adding direct KV-cache placement, folding the fixed RMSNorm gain into weights, writing FP8 output directly with delayed scaling, and supporting prefill without padding. Decode uses INT4 projection weights and an INT4 KV-cache copy. Weights and keys follow Tensor Core fragment layouts for direct dequantization into MMA operands without full intermediate tiles. A block-diagonal Hadamard transform reduces cache quantization error from outlier channels. On one H100, prefill is up to 1.48x faster than compiled PyTorch FP8 and reaches 1.29 PFLOP/s. For gate/up projection with SwiGLU at the 8B shape, our BF16 path is 1.13x faster than CODA. Our FP8 path is 2.02-2.18x faster than the evaluated BF16 CODA path. Across 8B and 70B shapes at batches 1-32, INT4 decode is 1.3-2.4x faster than the faster of PyTorch's BF16 and INT4 blocks at each point: 2.1-3.3x faster than compiled, CUDA-graphed BF16 and 1.3-6.3x faster than the same block using PyTorch's INT4 projection kernel, which targets a single query row and loses to BF16 at batch 32. It is also 31-51% faster than our FP8 path. Complete Llama-3.1-8B decode takes 2.8 ms per step at batch one, versus 8.1 ms for the compiled transformers implementation. Decoding every WikiText-2 token through the INT4 weight path raises perplexity from 6.24 to 7.23 with round-to-nearest weights or 6.99 with GPTQ in the same format; the rotated INT4 cache adds 0.20. The kernels match a quantized reference computation within 0.001 perplexity.</summary>

    <title>DrugHarness: An Evolvable Agent Harness for Computational Drug Discovery</title>
    <updated>2026-10-16T17:20:19Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23791v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23791v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Computational drug discovery requires agents to compose scientific operations and adapt to changing evidence and constraints. Here we introduce DrugHarness, an evolvable agent harness coupling composable scientific execution with conditional skill induction. Its environment integrates over 80 scientific operations, biomedical resources and task-specific code, preserving associations among candidates, results and artifacts. From execution trajectories and outcome feedback, DrugHarness induces action hypotheses with observable applicability conditions, recommended actions and supporting evidence. An independent review agent evaluates candidate skills derived from these hypotheses through source verification and, when needed, targeted execution trials. Admitted skills guide subsequent tasks and are revised through feedback. Evaluation on MolBench and SMDD-Bench demonstrates capabilities in molecular screening, optimization and constrained design. Without evolution, DrugHarness exceeds reported MolClaw-CC results by 10.8 percentage points in affinity-comparison accuracy and 55% in mean top-three active hits on MolBench. Retrospective evaluation on skill-development tasks shows that evolution increases Qwen's affinity-comparison accuracy from 62.2% to 81.1% and optimization success from 79.5% to 87.2%. In a prospective HPK1 study, DrugHarness achieves a more favorable median docking score than Biomni among system-specific candidates. A synthesized compound achieves a cellular IC50 of 14.19 nM, a 2.64-fold potency improvement over the best input reference, with activity competitive with two selected compounds designed by experienced medicinal chemists. These results support conditional skill evolution for scientific agents and demonstrate a workflow connecting computational drug design with experimental validation.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23788v1</id>
    <title>Parametric Resonance in Primal-Dual Learning for Slowly Non-Stationary Constrained MDPs</title>
    <updated>2026-10-16T17:19:08Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23788v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23788v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Primal-dual methods for constrained Markov decision processes are analyzed under a two-timescale assumption, with non-stationarity entering through two channels. In the additive channel, where the constraint level oscillates, the dual oscillation saturates at a floor set by the moving optimum and is amplified linearly by the timescale ratio. In the parametric channel, where the constraint sensitivity oscillates, a coherent modulation carries no resonant forcing at any depth: the dual update's stiffness modulation cancels the primal update's damping modulation. Instability instead comes from a mismatch between the constraint estimate used by the primal update and the measurement used by the dual update, producing a parametric resonance at twice the pair's natural frequency. The tolerated mismatch grows with the square root of the forcing bandwidth and collapses with the square root of the dual-to-primal step-size ratio. These results hold on the tangent linear-quadratic reduction around an active saddle, for one constraint and for $K$ constraints under a common modulation and an isotropy condition. Driving both updates from the same estimate removes the resonant forcing but introduces a stationary offset equal to the estimator's bias. In a Lagrangian soft actor-critic agent, the multiplier locks onto the sub-harmonic at the timescale ratios its identified linear loop predicts and a coherent cost critic suppresses the lock-in, while a proportional (PID) term, predicted to leave the lock-in in place, suppresses most of it through the projection of the multiplier.</summary>

    <summary>We present a transformer-based variational autoregressive network for sampling lattice systems with continuous degrees of freedom and apply it to the two-dimensional XY model near the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless transition.     <title>Transport and thermalization under noncommuting localized constraints</title>
    <updated>2026-10-16T17:15:04Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23781v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23781v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We investigate the effects of spatially localized conserved quantities on transport and thermalization in quantum and classical many-body systems. We consider several related models: the integrable quantum Volterra model, its nonintegrable classical limit, and two cellular automata derived from the latter. Although localized constraints are often associated with lattice gauge theories, our models do not admit such an interpretation. In systems with discrete degrees of freedom, these constraints induce uniform fragmentation of the Hilbert or configuration space. In the quantum Volterra model, we derive an exact mapping of the dynamics within each Hilbert-space fragment onto a quantum chiral Potts chain. We find that energy transport is ballistic, with identical transport coefficients across all fragments. In the nonintegrable classical limit, energy transport is diffusive, and we similarly find the diffusion constant to be independent of whether or not the constraints are fixed (resolved). Finally, in the cellular automata, we show that, despite leaving transport unaffected, localized constraints lead to a strong breakdown of local ergodicity.</summary>

    <title>Mesoscopic learning dynamics of extensive-width neural networks</title>
    <updated>2026-10-16T17:12:43Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23779v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23779v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Understanding how stochastic gradient descent learns internal representations in wide neural networks trained on rich target functions is a central problem in machine learning. We study this question in two-layer neural networks learning target functions represented by networks of the same architecture, with arbitrary nonlinearity, and with network width and input dimension growing proportionally. In this regime, standard approaches for describing the learning dynamics require tracking a diverging number of overlaps, which measure correlations between learned and target features, leaving no obvious description in terms of a few order parameters. Here, we develop a mesoscopic description of learning by characterizing the distribution of overlaps. In the early stages of learning, we find that a Gaussian description of overlap statistics reduces the learning dynamics to a few collective variables that track learning of the target function's linear and quadratic components. We then estimate the timescale of specialization, when Gaussian closure breaks down and individual learned features begin to strongly correlate with specific target features. We find that specialization in extensive-rank networks is accelerated via a quadratic shielding mechanism, whereby learning the linear and quadratic components of the target function filters gradient fluctuations. We finally describe how the activation function determines the pattern of specialization and characterize the subsequent refinement of learned features. Together, these results show how collective learning gives way to individual feature discovery and clarify when learning in large neural networks admits a simple statistical description.</summary>

    <title>Scaling of entanglement with distance between subsystems: detection of phase transitions in the $t'$-$π$-flux model</title>
    <updated>2026-10-16T17:08:03Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23770v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>

    <summary>The system-size scaling of bipartite entanglement can be used to detect phase transitions. We develop a related approach for strongly correlated electron models where large density matrices or large system size scaling are inaccessible. To this end, we demonstrate that phase transitions of various kinds are signaled by a sharp signature in the first- or second-order logarithmic derivatives of the negativity measuring entanglement between small clusters at varying distances. Crucially, we show how to mitigate the effect of quantum Monte Carlo noise at large distances when computing the negativity. Our focus is on the $t'$-$π$-flux Hubbard model using auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo simulations. It has the particular advantage of showing three distinct phase transitions in a single model: semimetal to band insulator, semimetal to antiferromagnetic Mott insulator, and a magnetic order-disorder transition belonging to the Gaussian, Gross-Neveu, and O(3) Wilson-Fisher universality classes, respectively.</summary>

    <title>Logic-Guided Graph Denoising Diffusion Models</title>
    <updated>2026-10-16T17:06:07Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23766v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23766v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Graph diffusion models are competitive approaches for generating complex graph-structured data. However, when such distributions have strict structural constraints, diffusion models may fail to capture them exactly, resulting in the generation of invalid graphs. In this paper, we propose a method for grounding graph diffusion models in domain-specific knowledge via First Order Logic (FOL), leveraging its expressive and interpretable formalism to impose structural constraints on the generative process. We incorporate domain knowledge using classifier guidance, a technique that conditions the diffusion model's distribution on external variables to exert control over the sampled data. During the generative process, classifier guidance steers the denoising trajectory to optimize an objective function, which we define as a fuzzy and differentiable relaxation of the logical rules. Our methodology requires only the specification of constraints in FOL, whose satisfaction is encouraged at inference time to guide a pre-trained generative model. We evaluate our approach by comparing the unconditional generation of knowledge graphs with our logic-guided framework, which incorporates domain ontologies as structural constraints during inference. This approach significantly increases the proportion of generated graphs that satisfy the ontological constraints.</summary>

    <summary>Weakly supervised anomaly detection on tabular data is an essential task in many label-scarce applications, since tabular data is widely encountered and it is commonly observed in practice that only a limited number of labeled anomalies are available alongside abundant unlabeled samples. Most existing methods try to learn features that capture the inherent distribution patterns in the target domain. However, such features often struggle to provide a complete description of possible abnormal characteristics and are highly susceptible to overfitting the extremely scarce labels. To address this challenge, we propose a weakly supervised anomaly detection method based on universal semantic enhancement for tabular data, which fuses the universal knowledge from a pre-trained tabular foundation model with the domain-specific knowledge learned on the target dataset. The two types of knowledge are naturally complementary: universal semantics describe the common patterns of tabular data across domains, while the domain-specific features capture the inherent distributions of normal and anomalous behaviors in the target dataset. A prototype-conditioned modulation mechanism is then designed to effectively integrate the two types of features, allowing them to reinforce each other for improved anomaly detection. Extensive experiments on public datasets show that the proposed method outperforms competitive methods when only eight labeled anomalies are available in the training procedure.</summary>

    <title>From Flow-Box Invariants to Global Conservation Laws: Machine Learning-Assisted Detection of Singularities and Near-Integrability</title>
    <updated>2026-10-16T17:02:39Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23760v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23760v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Conservation laws reveal invariant structure in dynamical systems and constrain their evolution to lower-dimensional level sets. Locally, however, per the flow-box theorem, every $d$-dimensional system generically admits $d-1$ functionally independent conservation laws near a regular point even though, generically, only a few such laws persist globally. Data-driven methods typically learn conservation laws on a prescribed region of phase space from which training samples are drawn, leaving their behavior beyond that region unresolved. We formulate this local-to-global continuation problem and develop an {expanding-domain neural deflation} framework that tracks the number of independent conservation laws over nested domains. The method recovers the expected $d-1$ local invariants and detects their successive breakdown as the domain expands, relaxing to the expected global conservation law limit. It distinguishes the local invariants (associated with Frobenius integrability) from persistent global structure and shows that the domain scale over which additional laws survive reflects proximity to Liouville integrability. Pointwise losses can localize isolated obstructions, whereas in more complicated dynamics the breakdown of our loss functions is gradual and spatially diffuse. The framework thus provides a data-driven approach for studying the persistence and breakdown of (so-far-learned) conservation laws across phase space.</summary>

    <title>LagNet: Lag-Structured Operators for Long-Term Time Series Forecasting</title>
    <updated>2026-10-16T16:44:53Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23735v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23735v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Long-term time series forecasting maps a finite history window to an extended future horizon. Many existing models focus primarily on the design of input representations and model structures, while paying less attention to the structural form of the history-to-future forecasting operator itself. We examine this operator directly and find that, across model families, sensitivity matrices exhibit recurring diagonal patterns whose diagonals correspond to relative temporal lags. Motivated by this observation, we develop a framework for direct multi-step forecasting based on lag-structured temporal operators. Its basic building block, LagLayer, constructs a Toeplitz matrix by tying history-to-future connections with the same relative lag and incorporates horizon-wise and history-wise scaling coefficients to relax exact sharing. This design enables LagLayer to serve as an effective replacement for temporal linear layers in existing forecasting models. Stacking LagLayer modules with activations and multiple feature maps yields LagNet. Experiments on long-term time series forecasting benchmarks show that our method is competitive with strong baselines, while sensitivity matrix diagnostics and limited-data experiments demonstrate that LagLayer provides an effective and sample-efficient alternative to a linear layer.</summary>

    <title>Bridging the Language Gap in Scholarly Data II: Enhancing Gender Inference for Chinese Names</title>
    <updated>2026-10-16T16:44:41Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23734v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23734v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Perceived gender inference from names is important for inclusive scientometrics research, yet existing methods perform poorly on non-Western scholars. We address this gap for Chinese names, which appear in two forms, Hanzi and Pinyin, its Romanized form (e.g., Zhang Wei, Li Na). In international bibliographic records, names are often available only in Pinyin. However, a single pinyin name can correspond to multiple distinct hanzi characters with different gender associations, so gender inference from Pinyin alone is intrinsically ambiguous. To address this, we first develop two hanzi models, a regression model that produces a continuous gender score from 0 (male) to 1 (female), and a classification model that outputs one of three labels (\em{male}, \em{neutral}, \em{female}). We train them on a sample of hanzi names from Chinese-language physics publications, rated by 11 native Chinese speakers. On this sample, the models achieve an RMSE of $0.09$ and an R$^2$ of $0.85$ (regression), and macro-AUC of $0.97$ and a Cohen's $κ$ of $0.81$ (classification), demonstrating high performance that is robust to class imbalance. For pinyin names, we propose a pipeline that aggregates hanzi predictions via transliteration and frequency weighting, together with an ambiguity score that flags names whose gender cannot be resolved from Pinyin alone. Benchmarked against three off-the-shelf tools (Namsor, GPT, and Claude), our models achieve the highest agreement with human annotations for both gender scores and gender labels, in both scripts. Applied to an independent sample of Chinese-named authors in APS journals, our models assign a gender to every name, whereas existing Pinyin-based methods leave between 20\% and 100\% of names unclassified. These findings demonstrate the importance of hanzi-level information for reliable gender inference of Chinese names. Code and data are publicly available.</summary>

    <title>Escaping Parameter Space: Tight Generalization Bounds via Representation Quality</title>
    <updated>2026-10-16T16:43:57Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23729v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>

    <summary>We derive a tight generalization bound for deterministic neural We derive a tight generalization bound for deterministic neural networks based on their last hidden layer representations. By evaluating representation quality with a parameter-free $k$-nearest-neighbor ($k$-NN) classifier, our certificate avoids traditional parameter-space complexity measures, KL divergences to a posterior, weight norms, and compression. The bound is tight: trained from scratch, it reaches an 8.0 percentage point gap to test error on CIFAR-10 (ResNet-18) and yields the first non-vacuous certificates we are aware of on CIFAR-100; with frozen DINOv2 representations, it certifies at 1.4\% on CIFAR-10 and 23.1\% on 1,000-class ImageNet. It decomposes additively into three empirical, independently measurable quantities: local class geometry ($k$-NN decoder error), decoder-network agreement, and training stability. This allows the bound to act as a diagnostic tool: we demonstrate that actively destroying local class geometry eliminates generalization while leaving dataset memorization intact, identifying class geometry as a causally relevant mechanism for generalization. Finally, we show that learned representations are significantly less sensitive to weight noise than linear readouts, suggesting why parameter-space certificates often struggle to remain tight.</summary>

    <title>ECG-SDI: Single-lead Electrocardiogram Enables Continuous Sleep Depth Index Profiling and Scalable Digital Biomarkers for Sleep Health</title>
    <updated>2026-10-16T16:43:07Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23727v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23727v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Conventional sleep staging provides a coarse-grained representation that obscures within-stage depth variation. We developed ECG-SDI, a single-lead electrocardiography (ECG) framework for continuous sleep-depth profiling and digital biomarker extraction. Using 12,392 overnight polysomnographic recordings, we trained and validated a two-stage deep learning model supervised by conventional sleep-stage labels. Correlations with ordered stages excluding rapid eye movement (REM) sleep were 0.828 in the pooled internal test set and 0.848 in the external Cleveland Family Study; corresponding REM classification AUROCs were 0.954 and 0.977. Overnight trajectories captured within-stage variation. Biomarker-based phenotyping identified a disturbed subtype associated with poorer subjective sleep quality and higher all-cause mortality in the Sleep Heart Health Study (adjusted hazard ratio, 1.20; 95% CI, 1.05-1.38). Among 507 participants with paired recordings before and after continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP), normalized sleep-depth area increased by 6.1% and shallow-sleep burden below 0.3 decreased by 16.0%. Exploratory analyses linked reductions in approximate entropy and depth variability to reduced oxygen desaturation and increased sleep efficiency, respectively (Spearman rho = 0.24 and 0.12); both associations remained positive after covariate adjustment. Mean ECG-SDI within N2 increased by 0.017 (95% CI, 0.004-0.030). A wearable proof-of-concept illustrated the acquisition-to-report workflow. These findings support ECG-based sleep phenotyping and further evaluation of CPAP response monitoring at home.</summary>

    <title>Beyond Large Language Models: A Mental World Model Framework for Mental Modeling, Simulation, Evolution, and Interpretability</title>
    <updated>2026-10-16T16:42:11Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23722v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23722v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Understanding and simulating how subjective cognition and mental states emerge, evolve, and shape behavior is essential for advancing artificial intelligence toward deeper social cognition and general intelligence. Existing large language models (LLMs) and Theory of Mind (ToM) methods primarily infer mental states from linguistic information, lacking unified mechanisms for subjective world construction, cognitive-psychological interactions, dynamic evolution, and historical dependencies. This paper introduces the Mental World Model (MWM) and its implementation, the Multi-Branch Mental Evolution Architecture (MMEA), which explicitly constructs subjective worlds, models interactions between cognition and mental states, and simulates continuous mental evolution shaped by historical experiences. On DynToM and RecToM, MMEA achieves 96.48% and 94.00% accuracy, respectively, outperforming leading LLMs and specialized ToM methods. Additional experiments demonstrate improvements of 28.7, 39.3, and 16.6 percentage points in mental state and behavior prediction, long-sequence prediction, and implicit mental state inference, respectively. The results demonstrate that MMEA provides an interpretable framework for continuous mental modeling, enabling AI to move beyond surface-level semantic representations to infer individuals' underlying mental states from linguistic information and dynamically simulate their internal cognitive processes and evolution over time. MWM also provides a promising foundation for causal reasoning, personalized AI, sustained human-AI interaction, and future advances toward artificial general intelligence (AGI).</summary>

    <title>Neural Expansion: A Unified Mechanism for How Deep Neural Networks Generalize</title>
    <updated>2026-10-16T16:38:02Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23716v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23716v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Deep neural networks demonstrate remarkable generalization despite being highly over-parameterized, challenging traditional statistical learning theories. While several theoretical paradigms such as margin-based bounds, PAC-Bayesian analyses, and neural tangent kernels provide global explanations, they often lack mechanistic insight into how generalization emerges from training dynamics. We introduce Neural Expansion, a unified geometric framework that characterizes generalization through the expansion of directionally-selective ray coverage in the input space. Using Generalization Intervals (GIs), we quantify direction-specific regions around training samples where the model's predictions remain stable. Our extensive empirical studies across diverse architectures and datasets reveal that training leads to progressive expansion of ray coverage, particularly along directions with low Jacobian singular values. This mechanism helps explain a large fraction of correctly classified test inputs, adversarial examples, and even mislabeled or out-of-distribution samples through the geometry of ray coverage rather than instance-level memorization. By connecting input-space curvature to predictive behavior, our framework provides a mechanistic foundation that complements existing global theories of deep learning.</summary>

    <title>GLOBE: Evolving Structured Agentic Memory for E-commerce Product Optimization in Generative Search</title>
    <updated>2026-10-16T16:33:17Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23709v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.23709v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Optimizing product listings for generative search requires language agents not only to rewrite effectively but also to continually self-improve by retaining successful strategies across diverse categories. However, existing approaches often treat structured listings as free-form text, leaving effective strategies implicit in prompts, search trajectories, or rewritten outputs rather than accumulating them as a reusable agentic memory. To address this limitation, we introduce GLOBE, an agentic framework that drives continual self-improvement by storing optimization knowledge in an evolving handbook of explicit, field-scoped behaviors. In each episode, an Editor applies relevant behaviors and receives rank-based feedback, which a Reflector converts into behavior updates. Crucially for dependable execution in real-world settings, a Moderator removes redundant proposals, a Curator commits accepted changes, and consistently harmful behaviors are deactivated. This cycle transforms episodic feedback into a persistent, field-scoped optimization memory. Experiments show that structured behaviors outperform monolithic prompt optimization, while feedback-driven evolution and moderation further improve effectiveness and reduce downside risk. The learned behaviors also remain effective on unseen product categories, suggesting that agentic memory evolution supports interpretable and transferable product optimization.</summary>

    <summary>A multi-step agent task fails when a single tool it needs is missing, yet the tools an agent may need are too many to list: the roughly 8,200 tools on the platform we study have definitions that together exceed the context window of any model we evaluate. We present Tool Recommendation, a deployed system that gives an agent all of them, hundreds of times more than a typical MCP server exposes, through a fixed interface of three tools. It runs at the gateway between agent and tools, executing every call under the end user's own credentials and checking it against the user's consent for each service and the tools the agent may use. We evaluate it on both a public retrieval benchmark and billed end-to-end session cost. On ToolRet, Tool Recommendation places every tool a query needs in the top ten 57% more often than BM25, a lexical ranking that commercial tool search offers, and compares favorably with published systems up to nine times its size. In paired multi-step workflows, its first recommendation covered every required tool in 93% of Codex sessions, and against a fixed list of 100 tools it cut input tokens by 17% with Codex and 40% with Claude Code and the total bill in all 14 runs, by up to 40%, with no change in task completion.</summary>

    <summary>Diffusion-based protein structure prediction models produce all-atom structures in about 200 denoising steps, and that cost has driven a number of few-step samplers. We present Blitz, a few-step distillation framework that uses a geometric noise schedule to distribute steps more evenly across noise scales, then learns those updates through multistep consistency training. Because published few-step results use different benchmarks and scoring procedures, we compare both distilled models with their teachers and other few-step methods under a common evaluation protocol covering structural accuracy, interface quality, ligand placement, and stereochemical validity.     <title>Equivalence testing and run-count design for stochastic machine-learning experiments</title>
    <updated>2026-10-16T16:28:12Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23700v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>

    <summary>Claims that two training methods perform equally well often rest on a non-significant difference between two or three runs per method. We develop a protocol, with its power theory, for certifying practical equivalence in per-run metrics such as the AUROC (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve). It rests on a two-level (seed x item) variance model separating between-run dispersion from item-level noise. Equivalence within a pre-specified margin is tested by two one-sided tests (TOST), equivalently by a confidence interval inside the margin; a two-level bootstrap covers composite statistics. A closed-form formula converts a margin and a target power into runs per method; its shifted-t refinement is calibrated against the realised two-level process. Simulations on a 270-cell grid and under non-Gaussian seed laws confirm the formula within its design-relevant range, from five runs per method. For four published runs of a joint energy-based model, the failure to certify equivalence was largely decided by design: with the variance calibrated to those runs, two per method certify with probability near three per cent, whereas certifying 0.01 AUROC at 80 per cent power needs twelve even under exact equality. A second case study on a thousand-seed CIFAR-10 zoo and the MultiBERTs checks the formula against real seed laws (within 0.05 in that range) and resolves comparisons that two or three runs leave undecided. In a two-stage design (pilot, then formula), our experiments suggest that an upper confidence bound on the pilot variance substantially reduces the undersizing seen with its point estimate.</summary>

    <title>Recursive Operator Localization and Spectral Gap Descent via the Geometry of Local Spectral Expansion</title>
    <updated>2026-10-16T16:23:52Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.23695v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>

    <summary>We introduce Recursive Operator Localization (ROL), a framework for constructing hierarchies of local energy problems linked by linear maps between Hilbert spaces. To address spectral-gap problems, including those arising in quantum systems, we study a realization of ROL by nested subspaces indexed by a weighted simplicial complex. Using spectral gaps of auxiliary classical random walks on links, we propagate geometric estimates upward and use them to turn local spectral gaps at the bottom of the hierarchy into a spectral-gap bound for the global operator. For weighted scalar-valued functions on facets, the ROL decomposition becomes the law of total variance, recovering classical spectral-gap bounds from local link expansion (Alev and Lau, STOC 2020). Moreover, for positive binary spin distributions, conditional influence describes the overlap of the corresponding subspaces, yielding known heat-bath gap bounds from spectral independence (Anari, Liu, and Oveis Gharan, FOCS 2020). The framework also offers a route toward quantum Gibbs sampling, with applications requiring model-specific geometric estimates and energy comparisons.</summary>

The EAP regimen consists of etoposide, cytarabine, and pegylated granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (pegfilgrastim) and is used for hematopoietic stem cell mobilization before autologous stem cell transplantation in patients with multiple myeloma and B-cell lymphoma.

Severe thrombocytopenia is a common complication during EAP-based stem cell mobilization and may increase the risk of bleeding and the need for platelet transfusions, and may sometimes delay stem cell collection. {"protocolSection":{"identificationModule":{"nctId":"NCT07185672","orgStudyIdInfo":{"id":"TMCIEC3258"},"organization":{"fullName":"Tata Memorial Hospital","class":"OTHER_GOV"},"briefTitle":"PRRT Versus PRRT Plus Chemotherapy in GEP NET (PReCedeNT Trial)","officialTitle":"PReCedeNT Trial: Phase III Randomised Controlled Open Label Trial of Lutetium 177 PRRT Plus Chemotherapy Versus PRRT Aalone in FDG Avid Well Differentiated Gastroenteropancreatic Neuroendocrine Tumors","acronym":"PReCedeNT"},"statusModule":{"statusVerifiedDate":"2025-09","overallStatus":"RECRUITING","expandedAccessInfo":{"hasExpandedAccess":false},"startDateStruct":{"date":"2019-08-07","type":"ACTUAL"},"primaryCompletionDateStruct":{"date":"2027-08-07","type":"ESTIMATED"},"completionDateStruct":{"date":"2027-08-07","type":"ESTIMATED"},"studyFirstSubmitDate":"2025-08-25","studyFirstSubmitQcDate":"2025-09-17","studyFirstPostDateStruct":{"date":"2025-09-22","type":"ACTUAL"},"lastUpdateSubmitDate":"2025-09-17","lastUpdatePostDateStruct":{"date":"2025-09-22","type":"ACTUAL"}},"sponsorCollaboratorsModule":{"responsibleParty":{"type":"PRINCIPAL_INVESTIGATOR","investigatorFullName":"Ameya Puranik","investigatorTitle":"Professor","investigatorAffiliation":"Tata Memorial Hospital"},"leadSponsor":{"name":"Tata Memorial Hospital","class":"OTHER_GOV"}},"oversightModule":{"oversightHasDmc":true,"isFdaRegulatedDrug":false,"isFdaRegulatedDevice":false},"descriptionModule":{"briefSummary":"Neuroendocrine tumours (NETs), better defined as neoplasms (NENs), are a heterogeneous group of neoplasms that range from well-differentiated tumours to more aggressive carcinomas. Peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (PRRT) with Lutetium-177 DOTATATE is the established standard of care for patients with well-differentiated metastatic or locally advanced GEP-NETs. It has demonstrated a significant improvement in outcomes compared to Octreotide LAR, both as a first-line and second-line treatment approach, following the results of NETTER-1 and NETTER-2 trials, respectively. ENETS guidelines recommend the use of Ga-68 labeled DOTANOC/TOC/TATAE imaging only for WHO Grade 1 NET whereas FDG PET is the preferred modality for WHO Grade 3 NEN and NEC. For Grade 2 tumors (Mib index ranging from 3-20%), there are no strong recommendations for the addition of FDG PETCT in existing diagnostic algorithm. FDG PET positivity has been shown to be an independent predictor of shorter progression-free and overall survival in NET patients undergoing peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (PRRT). (8) Consequently, it is imperative to address FDG-avid tumors by integrating PRRT and chemotherapy. There are no strong recommendations for the grade wise management of GEP-NETs particularly grade 2 \& 3. Although recently published NETTER 2 trial substantiated the role of PRRT as a first line treatment for advanced grade GEP-NETs, still there is lack of evidence supporting the addition of chemotherapy in management of GEP-NETs. Given the absence of a prospective study to establish this treatment regimen, we designed a Phase 3 Randomized Controlled Trial to evaluate the combination of PRRT and CAPE-TEM-based chemotherapy in patients with FDG-positive metastatic well-differentiated NETs.","detailedDescription":"Neuroendocrine tumors (NETs) are a heterogeneous group of malignancies ranging from well- differentiated, slowly growing tumors to poorly differentiated neoplasms, which are aggressive and less frequent. Neuroendocrine cells have the ability to express several peptide receptors in high volumes, especially somatostatin receptors, which are heptahelical G-protein-coupled glycoprotein transmembrane receptors. In the most recent SEER register (SEER-17), more than half of all NETs, i.e. 61%, were gastroenteropancreatic neuroendocrine tumors (GEP-NETs), with the highest frequency being found in the rectum (17.7%), the small intestine (17.3%), and the colon (10.1%) . The tumor biology varies with the location of the primary tumors as well as with the grade and staging of the tumors. The malignant potential ranges from the most benign types of tumor to small intestinal tumors and up to neuroendocrine carcinoma (NEC) with very malignant behavior. The tumors are graded according to the classification system of the World Health Organization (WHO), wherein a new classification system is just being accepted. The tumors are divided into grade 1 NET (NET-G1), with a proliferation \<3%, NET-G2 with a proliferation between 3 and 20%, NET-G3, which is a new group with a Ki-67 \>20%, and finally NEC-G3, exhibiting a Ki-67 of \>20% as well (unpublished data). Of note, the difference between NET-G3 and NEC-G3 is mainly the degree of differentiation. NET-G3 are well-differentiated tumors, often with expression of somatostatin receptors. NEC-G3 are poorly differentiated tumors that usually lack expression of somatostatin receptors.

NETs are characterized by a general lack of symptoms until they are in advanced phase, and early biomarkers are not as available and useful as required. Heterogeneity is an intrinsic, pivotal feature of NETs that derives from diverse causes and ultimately shapes tumor fate. The different layers that conform NET heterogeneity include a wide range of distinct characteristics, from the mere location of the tumor to its clinical and functional features, and from its cellular properties, to the core signaling and (epi)genetic components defining the molecular signature of the tumor. The importance of this heterogeneity resides in that it translates into a high variability among tumors and, hence, patients, which hinders a more precise diagnosis and prognosis and more efficacious treatment of these diseases. Heterogeneity can be assessed objectively by molecular imaging techniques. Patients with well- differentiated GEP NETs undergo imaging with Ga-68-DOTATOC PET/CT (DOTA PET/CT), which is a somatostatin-receptor (SSTR)-specific imaging tracer. PET/CT with 68Ga-DOTA-peptides has been reported to present a higher sensitivity for the detection of well-differentiated, less aggressive NETs than well tolerated with negligible grade 3/4 toxicities. After a median follow-up period of 36 months, the median OS was not achieved with a median PFS of 48 months. At 3 months after completion of combination of PRRT and chemotherapy, 2% of patients showed a complete anatomical response, 28% a partial response, 68% stable disease, and only 2% progression. On FDG PET/CT, 27% achieved a complete metabolic response during the follow-up period. A biochemical response (\>25% fall in chromogranin-A levels) was seen in 45%. These results established the effectiveness of the combination of PRRT and chemotherapy which is now practiced routinely. However, there is no prospective study to establish this treatment regime. The investigators therefore propose to prospectively evaluate the combination of PRRT and chemotherapy in patients with well-differentiated NETs, in a systematic manner to generate reliable conclusions with regards to this treatment regimen for intermediate to high grade NETs. On the other hand, 18F-FDG PET/CT is preferred for more aggressive, less differentiated NETs as there is emerging evidence that the presence of increased expression of GLUT (glucose-transporter) receptors in NETs highlights an increased propensity for invasion and metastasis, and an overall poorer prognosis. In fact, a strong association has recently been shown between higher 18F-FDG uptake and worse outcome even in patients with well-differentiated or low-grade tumors, with provision of prognostic information independently of the mitotic rate. Accordingly, 18F-FDG has an important role in managing patients with NETs because of its high prognostic value and its higher sensitivity in delineating disease extent, especially in aggressive and high-grade and aggressive intermediate-grade tumors. While DOTA PET avidity is a feature of well-differentiated disease, FDG avidity tends to be associated with more aggressive, de-differentiated disease. Grade 1 NET tends to be DOTA-avid but negative on FDG PET, whereas grade 3 NEC generally shows the opposite imaging phenotype. Grade 2 NET may demonstrate uptake of both tracers. Irrespective of pathological grade, the distribution of these tracers may not be spatially concordant, with some lesions having either DOTA or FDG avidity, but not both. This highlights the limitations of relying on histopathological grade from a single biopsy site to predict disease behavior. Despite the prognostic utility of pathological grading, FDG PET positivity has been consistently shown to be independently associated with a poor prognosis. SSTR expression on the surface of NET enables the use of somatostatin analogues labelled with particle-emitting radionuclides for targeted peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (PRRT) NETTER-1 trial has established Lu-177 PRRT as standard of care in treatment of metastatic well-differentiated GEP NETs. However, FDG positivity in these tumors suggests presence of aggressive phenotypes and warrants simultaneous use of chemotherapy. Strosberg et.al, have shown exceptionally high and durable response rate with combination of Capecitabine and temozolomide in metastatic well, or moderately differentiated pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor. In contrast, periods of inactivity such as bed rest or immobilization result in losses of skeletal muscle size and strength. However, individuals experience variable magnitudes of muscle size change in response to changes in mechanical tension, such that certain individuals experience large changes in muscle mass whereas others do not. What is not currently known, and will be the primary goal of the present investigation, is to determine whether individuals who gain the most muscle mass with exercise training also lose the most muscle when they are immobilized. The investigators hypothesize that individuals who gain the most muscle with training will also lose the most with immobilization.","detailedDescription":"Resistance exercise, paired with protein ingestion, leads to the accretion of muscle proteins that over time results in the augmentation of muscle size and muscle strength. By virtue of its ability to stimulate increases in muscle size and strength, resistance exercise is an effective method that can be used by healthcare practitioners to promote the recovery of lost muscle mass resulting from a period of immobilization (resulting from broken bones, elective surgery, etc.). However, while exercise in general is an effective therapeutic strategy to combat muscle loss and frailty, the extent to which individuals respond to resistance exercise is highly variable. Some individuals exhibit large changes in muscle size (high responders) whereas other exhibit little to no change (low responders). Thus, where as one resistance exercise program might be an appropriate treatment for one individual following disuse, another individual might require a greater stimulus and/or pharmaceutical assistance in order to fully recover. What is currently unknown is whether individuals who experience the most profound increases in skeletal muscle mass following resistance exercise also lose the most muscle upon limb immobilization. Answering this gap in our knowledge will be the primary goal of this study. The procurement of this knowledge will hopefully permit the development of individualized exercise programs that can be used to influence the recovery of skeletal muscle that is lost with inactivity and immobilization."},"conditionsModule":{"conditions":["Muscle Atrophy","Disuse Atrophy (Muscle) of Lower Leg"],"keywords":["Muscle Hypertrophy","Muscle Atrophy","Resistance Training","Immobilization"]},"designModule":{"studyType":"INTERVENTIONAL","phases":["NA"],"designInfo":{"allocation":"RANDOMIZED","interventionModel":"SINGLE_GROUP","interventionModelDescription":"The model will be a within-subject intervention.
